It names who does it: records' flush returns state 'failed' with that error; the survey passes that error on from its opening flush (survey.md D11) and raises WorktreeError('not_permitted') from its worktree library with the same words (D20); step 4 builds on them (its ORDER.md rule 7). delivery.md D6: both strategies now end in an explicit 'git commit -F <file>' ('squash' after 'git merge --squash', 'merge' after 'git merge --no-ff --no-commit'), so the project's pre-commit and commit-msg hooks run whatever the strategy, and pre-merge-commit never runs because the tool makes no automatic merge commit. The other option, stating different hooks per strategy, was rejected: a project's pre-commit would be skipped silently under 'merge'. D7: a commit git refuses is 'refused' and names 'git hook <names>' (those of pre-commit, prepare-commit-msg and commit-msg that are executable in the worktree's hooks directory), or 'git' when there is none; row 13's text carries it. Step-4 ORDER.md rule 7 states what a hook sees there (cwd = the worktree, that worktree's GIT_DIR, tracked files only). D10: a clean merge-in whose commit git refuses is aborted with 'git merge --abort' and answered as D7, so the story branch is as it was. Tests: test_both_strategies_run_pre_commit_never_pre_merge_commit, test_hook_rejection_refuses_and_moves_nothing (now naming the hook and merging on the next call), test_refused_merge_in_commit_is_aborted. To stay under the size limit, sentences that ORDER.md sections 5 and 7 already carry were replaced by pointers.
